name: Web Bot Auth, and its Signature Agent Card. IETF individual drafts by Thibault Meunier and Sandor Major (Cloudflare): draft-meunier-web-bot-auth-architecture (versions 00–05, expired, superseded), draft-meunier-webbotauth-httpsig-protocol (currently -02, Standards Track intent), and draft-meunier-webbotauth-registry (currently -03, published 26 June 2026). Cloudflare markets the deployment as 'Verified Bots with cryptography' / 'message-signature verified bots'. Built on RFC 9421 (HTTP Message Signatures) and RFC 7517 (JWKS).
kind: Standards-track proposal plus a shipped commercial service. Neither one nor the other cleanly: the protocol is an individual IETF draft that no working group has adopted, while the verification side is already deployed at CDN scale by a single vendor. The 'standard' and the 'service' are being built by the same party, which is the central fact to hold on to when reading anything about it.
maturity: Shipped before standardised, and the gap is wide. As of 2026 no IETF working group has adopted a single draft; the httpsig-protocol draft carries Standards Track intent and expires February 2027, the registry draft expires December 2026, and the original architecture draft has already expired and been superseded. Meanwhile verification is live: Cloudflare has it in the Verified Bots Program for Free and Pro plans with Business and Enterprise staged behind validation, and AWS WAF, Vercel, Shopify and Akamai are reported as having implemented support, with Visa TAP and Mastercard Agent Pay adopting it as an authentication foundation for agentic payments. The registry side firmed up in February 2026 with Cloudflare and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore announcing a common open registry format for agent public-key discovery. Practically: the wire format is stable enough to implement against, the governance is not settled, and the risk is single-vendor definition rather than obsolescence.
license: The drafts are IETF documents under the BSD-style IETF Trust Legal Provisions, freely implementable. RFC 9421 and RFC 7517 likewise. Cloudflare's reference implementations and the web-bot-auth tooling are open source under permissive licenses [uncertain — exact SPDX per repository not verified]. There is no licensing obstacle whatsoever; the costs of adoption are operational (running a key directory, publishing a card, holding a private key) rather than legal.
keeps_and_discards: This is not an extraction approach and touches no page content. It operates strictly on the request: the client signs a covered component set — typically the target URI's authority, the method, the path, and the Signature-Agent header value — with an Ed25519 private key, and attaches Signature-Input and Signature headers per RFC 9421. What it 'keeps' is a verifiable assertion of who is asking; what it discards is the anonymity of the request. Its effect on extraction is entirely upstream and entirely about access: it determines whether the origin serves the real document, a degraded one, a 402, or a challenge. In a corpus where a meaningful fraction of origins sit behind Cloudflare, that is the largest single determinant of what enters the fold, and it is a determinant this project currently exercises no control over.
structure_preserved: No document structure is involved. The one structural artifact it introduces is the Signature Agent Card itself, a JSON document at a well-known path — https://<agent-domain>/.well-known/signature-agent-card — with a defined field set: client_name, client_uri, logo_uri, contacts, expected-user-agent, rfc9309-product-token, rfc9309-compliance, trigger (fetcher vs crawler), purpose, targeted-content, known-urls, rate-control, rate-expectation, and keys (a JWKS). At least one parameter must be set; unknown parameters must be ignored. Key material lives separately at /.well-known/http-message-signature-directory as a JSON Web Key Set. Both are small, stable, machine-readable documents that a sensor could fold trivially, though there is little reason to.
interactive_elements: None. Web Bot Auth has no interaction model — it is a per-request header triple, evaluated at the edge before any content is generated. The only sense in which it touches interactivity is the one that matters most for an agentic project: the rfc9309-compliance and trigger fields let an agent declare whether it is a fetcher acting on a user's immediate behalf or a crawler operating autonomously, and origins are expected to treat those differently. That distinction — user-triggered fetch versus autonomous crawl — is the axis on which most emerging access policy turns, and this project's sensor sits ambiguously across it.
interactive_state_fidelity: No effect on disabled / checked / selected / expanded or ARIA state, and no token cost. The indirect effect is the familiar one: a verified agent is more likely to receive a fully-served, fully-hydrated page than an unverified one, so state fidelity is preserved by preserving normal service rather than by any representational choice. There is a countervailing possibility that deserves stating and has not been measured: an origin that knows it is serving an AI agent may deliberately serve a reduced or differently-structured page — a text-only view, a summary, a licensing notice — in which case declaring agency degrades fidelity rather than improving it. No published measurement of how origins differentiate content for verified agents exists yet, and this is the single most important unknown for a project considering adoption. [uncertain]
layout_awareness: None whatsoever; it is a transport-layer mechanism. This is a clean property relative to the project's constraints and needs no qualification.
javascript_required: No. Signing happens at the HTTP client layer and verification at the CDN edge, both before any script runs. This is a genuine architectural advantage over every other item in the privacy category: it is the only mechanism here that establishes identity WITHOUT the page running script to interrogate the browser. An origin that trusts a signature does not need to fingerprint, which is the whole point — Web Bot Auth is proposed explicitly as the replacement for the detection arms race. For a project committed to running real pages with real scripts, it does not reduce script execution, but it does remove the incentive for the origin's anti-bot bundle to escalate.
evaluation_method: There is no evaluation in the research sense — there is no accuracy claim to evaluate, because cryptographic verification is not a heuristic. Either the signature validates against the published key and the covered components match, or it does not. What can be and has not been rigorously established is deployment-side behaviour: what fraction of origins actually check signatures, what they do differently when one validates, and whether declaring agency improves or degrades the content received. Cloudflare's evidence is deployment-existence (their own Radar URL Scanner runs as a verified bot under the scheme) plus adopter announcements, which is evidence of availability rather than of effect. The correct evaluation for this project is a differential one it can run itself: fold a set of origins with and without a valid signature and compare content, status codes and fold size.
corpus_size_and_origins: No corpus exists. Deployment breadth is asserted through vendor and adopter announcements rather than measured: Cloudflare (Free and Pro tiers live, Business and Enterprise staged), AWS WAF, Vercel, Shopify, Akamai, plus the Visa TAP and Mastercard Agent Pay integrations. None of these is a measurement of the open web. The relevant denominators — what share of the top-1M enforces or even reads Signature-Agent, what share of AI-crawler traffic is signed — are unpublished. Cloudflare's general CDN share puts a ceiling on how much of the web could be checking today, and it is a large minority of commercial sites and near-zero of small independent ones. Anything stated about prevalence here is inference. [uncertain]
reported_precision_recall: Not applicable and it is worth being explicit about why, because it is the mechanism's chief virtue. Signature verification has no false-positive or false-negative rate in the statistical sense: forging a signature requires the private key. The residual error modes are operational, not probabilistic — key compromise, clock skew pushing a request outside its nbf/exp window, a stale or unreachable key directory, or an origin misconfiguring its check. Every other identity mechanism in this research set is a probability estimate; this one is a proof. That difference is the strongest argument for it.
independent_oracle: Yes, and unusually strong: the cryptography is the oracle and it shares no assumptions with any party's beliefs about what a bot looks like. Domain control over the key directory path anchors the identity to something externally verifiable. The parts NOT covered by that oracle are the parts that carry all the risk, and they are pure assertion: the Signature Agent Card's purpose, targeted-content, rate-expectation and rfc9309-compliance fields are self-declared, unverified, and unenforceable — an agent can sign a request truthfully while its card lies about what it does with the data. The signature proves who, never what. Reputation systems built on top will have to supply the missing oracle, and that reintroduces exactly the opaque, vendor-controlled judgement the scheme was meant to replace.
evidence_independence: Weak in a specific and structural way: Cloudflare authored the drafts, operates the largest verifier, runs a verified bot under the scheme, and publishes most of the available analysis. That is not fraud, and the drafts are technically sound and openly developed — but the standard, the deployment, the registry format and the commentary all originate with one company that also sells bot mitigation and, separately, pay-per-crawl. The IETF has not adopted the work, which is the normal check on exactly this, and until a working group does, 'the standard' is one vendor's proposal with adopters. The AWS/Bedrock AgentCore registry collaboration is the first meaningful second party. Treat adoption claims and effectiveness claims from vendor blogs as marketing until an independent measurement exists.
page_archetype_coverage: Not measured, and the deployment skew is the inverse of what a research-oriented corpus would want. Signature checking exists where anti-bot products exist: commercial, e-commerce, media, ticketing, finance. Documentation sites, public archives, government and academic pages — the archetypes least likely to challenge a crawler — are also the least likely to have any Web Bot Auth support, so adopting it buys nothing there. Concretely: on the kind of corpus this project appears to read, signing requests would be a no-op almost everywhere, and would matter only at the commercial tail. That makes adoption cheap to trial and low-reward in the short term, while being the correct long-term posture.
script_and_locale_behaviour: Fully script- and locale-invariant; it operates on HTTP headers and Ed25519 signatures over byte strings. One narrow note: the covered-component set includes the request target, so internationalised domain names and percent-encoded paths must be canonicalised identically by signer and verifier, and RFC 9421's canonicalisation rules govern that. Mismatched canonicalisation of non-ASCII paths is a plausible interoperability bug class, though no reports of it were located. [uncertain]
leaks_outward: This is the mechanism's defining trade and it must be stated plainly: Web Bot Auth deliberately and irrevocably discloses identity. Every signed request tells the origin which agent operator is asking, links that request to a published card describing purpose and expected behaviour, and makes every request from that key attributable and correlatable across every origin that verifies it. That is total, permanent, cross-site linkability — precisely the outcome the fingerprint-linkability item treats as the threat. The difference is consent and symmetry: the disclosure is deliberate, its content is chosen and published by the discloser, and it replaces an involuntary probabilistic identification with a voluntary exact one. Whether that is a privacy improvement depends entirely on whose privacy is being discussed. For a corpus-reading project it means abandoning any pretence of anonymous reading — but the fingerprint-linkability evidence shows that pretence was already thin (over 50 days of linkability from static fingerprints alone), so the honest accounting is that signing converts a leaky, deniable, involuntary identification into an exact, accountable, voluntary one at modest marginal cost.
mechanism_detectability: Detectability is not a risk here, it is the product — the entire mechanism exists to be detected, and 'is the page able to tell it is being read by an agent' is answered yes, by construction and by intent. That inverts the framing of the project's first tension in a way that dissolves it. If the sensor signs its requests, then navigator.webdriver being true costs nothing, because automation is already declared; the Marionette exposure stops being a leak and becomes redundant with a fact already asserted. And the attachShadow refusal then rests entirely on the grounds that actually hold it up — honouring an author's explicit encapsulation boundary, avoiding a permanent race against page scripts, and avoiding the cross-realm patching burden that CreepJS-style consistency sweeps would expose anyway. In other words: adopting Web Bot Auth is the move that makes the project's existing constraint set internally consistent, at the price of anonymity it does not actually have. That is the cleanest resolution available to the first tension, and it is a positive recommendation rather than a compromise. The one genuinely new detectability consideration is second-order and worth naming: a signed request is attributable, so an origin can serve THIS agent differently from all others, and any content differentiation aimed specifically at the signing key is invisible from a single capture — the cross-identity diff remains necessary, and now needs a signed and an unsigned identity rather than two anonymous ones.
countermeasures: For an agent operator wanting to limit what signing discloses, the levers are: publish a minimal card (the spec requires at least one parameter, not a full disclosure); use distinct keys for distinct activities so that a research crawl is not linked to unrelated traffic; rotate keys on a defined schedule; and sign selectively — the scheme does not require signing every request, so an agent can sign where signing buys access and omit it elsewhere. Selective signing is legitimate under the protocol but ethically ambiguous, since omitting a signature where an origin expects one is a return to the detection arms race. From the origin's side the countermeasure to a lying card is reputation and revocation, which the drafts gesture at without specifying; the registry draft's privacy considerations section is literally 'TODO', which is a fair summary of how developed that side is.
measured_fidelity_cost: No fidelity cost to the capture in the representational sense — no DOM change, no request blocking, no script suppression. Against this project's measured baseline, signing should sit at or below the 0.07% null-control floor on saved pages (it changes nothing about a saved page) and near zero on live sites, since it neither blocks nor rewrites requests. It therefore belongs in an entirely different category from block_trackers' 10.49% live cost, which is content suppression. The unmeasured and potentially large cost is the content-differentiation one: if some origins serve verified agents a reduced page, the fidelity cost of signing is not zero but negative-valued at those origins, and it is measurable with exactly the experiment the project already has the harness for — the same URLs, signed and unsigned, fold sizes compared against the corpus baseline. That experiment does not appear to have been run by anyone publicly, and it is cheap.
gate_state_at_capture: Web Bot Auth is best understood as making gate state legible and negotiable rather than as removing gates. A signed request that receives 200 with full content, a signed request that receives a 402 pay-per-crawl response, and an unsigned request that receives a challenge are three distinct, recordable gate states, and the signature is what makes them distinguishable — without it, a challenge and a paywall and a degraded serve all look like 'the page was different'. This is a direct and cheap improvement to the project's gate-state ledger: signing turns an ambiguous access outcome into an explicit, header-carried one. It also makes 402 responses interpretable rather than mysterious.
determinism: Fully deterministic given key, covered components and timestamp: the same request signed with the same key at the same instant produces the same signature, and verification is a pure function. The nondeterminism is temporal — signatures carry created and expires parameters, so a replayed request outside its window fails validation correctly, and clock skew between signer and verifier is the one place where identical inputs give different outcomes. Ed25519 signing is deterministic by design (no per-signature nonce), which removes an entire class of randomness that ECDSA would have introduced.
determinism_across_versions: Good and improving. RFC 9421 is a published RFC and stable; JWKS via RFC 7517 is long-settled. The volatile layer is the Web Bot Auth drafts themselves — the architecture draft already expired and was superseded, and the registry draft's parameter set is still growing under a Specification Required IANA policy. Field names in the Signature Agent Card should be expected to change before the work is adopted by a working group. The wire format (three headers, Ed25519, a JWKS at a well-known path) has been stable across the deployment period and is the part safe to build on; the card's schema is not.
reproducibility: The cryptographic verification is perfectly reproducible offline given the request, the covered components and the public key. What is not reproducible is any claim about how origins BEHAVE toward signed requests, since that depends on remote, mutable, per-origin configuration that no one publishes. A measured result of the form 'signing improved capture success on N origins' is a snapshot with the same shelf-life problem the anti-bot items have, and must be dated.
failure_modes: Ordered by likelihood. Clock skew pushing a request outside its created/expires window — the most common operational failure in every message-signing deployment. Key directory unreachable, stale, or served with the wrong content type, causing verification to fail open or closed depending on the verifier. Canonicalisation mismatch on the covered component set, especially with proxies that rewrite headers or normalise paths — any intermediary that alters a signed component invalidates the signature. Key compromise, which is catastrophic and for which the drafts specify no rotation protocol beyond nbf/exp validity windows. Card lying, where the signature validates and the declared purpose is false, which the protocol cannot detect at all. And the systemic one: an origin that verifies the signature and then decides it does not want this agent, which is a successful protocol run and a failed capture.
failure_visibility: Loud on the cryptographic path and silent on the policy path, and the split matters. A failed signature produces a definite, attributable outcome — Cloudflare's documented behaviour is to fall back to its existing bot identification and mitigation, so verification failure degrades into the ordinary detection regime rather than producing an error, which is quiet in exactly the wrong way: a misconfigured signer looks like an unsigned bot rather than like a broken one, so the operator learns nothing. That is a real design flaw for a client, and the mitigation is a positive control — an endpoint the operator runs that echoes whether the signature validated — rather than inferring success from the absence of a challenge. On the policy path, an origin serving reduced content to a verified agent is entirely silent, and only cross-identity comparison detects it.
scale_limits: Signing cost is one Ed25519 signature per request — microseconds, negligible against any network round trip, and comfortably linear. Verification is one signature check plus a cached key-directory lookup, which is why CDNs were willing to deploy it at edge scale. There is no superlinear regime in the cryptography. The non-linear costs are governance: key directory availability becomes a hard dependency of the whole crawl, and a single expired or unreachable directory silently downgrades every request. At 3,082 requests per run, the marginal cryptographic cost is invisible; the marginal risk of a directory outage is not.
delta_cost_model: Not applicable to page representation. Per-request cost is constant and independent of page size, which is the right shape and better than most items here — it does not scale with the document at all. Nothing about signing falls outside a per-request constant, so there is no out-of-model change class on the client side. On the origin side the analogous question — how often a verifier re-fetches a key directory and whether a rotated key invalidates in-flight sessions — is underspecified in the drafts. [uncertain]
reanchoring_stability: No node-identity model. The one durable-identity concept it contributes is the agent's own: the key pair plus the well-known card location is a stable, rotatable identity anchored to domain control, which survives IP changes, user-agent changes, and browser upgrades — every drift axis that defeats fingerprint-based identification. That is worth noting as the structural contrast with FP-STALKER: where fingerprint linkability achieves ~51 days of continuity by inference over drifting attributes, a signing key achieves indefinite continuity by declaration, and the operator controls when it breaks. Declared identity is simply a better-engineered version of the thing trackers spend enormous effort inferring.
adversarial_exposure: Preserves no page content and conceals nothing, so it adds no invisible-content exposure. Two contributions to the safety picture are worth recording. First, it opens a new and under-discussed attack surface in the opposite direction: the Signature Agent Card is a JSON document fetched from a third-party domain, and a verifier that renders or reasons over card fields (client_name, purpose, contacts) is consuming attacker-controlled text — which is an indirect prompt injection vector into any origin-side system that summarises agent cards with a model. The drafts' privacy considerations section being 'TODO' suggests this has not been analysed. Second and more usefully, signing makes an agent accountable, which changes the incentive landscape around injection: a site that detects an injection attempt against an identified agent can report it to a named operator, which is impossible against an anonymous one. Accountability is a weak defence but it is the only structural one in this research set.
provenance_carrying: It carries request-level provenance, not token-level: who asked, when, under which key, with which declared purpose. That is a genuine and complementary addition to the project's url : xpath : markdown : content key — the key answers 'where did this text come from in the document', while the signature answers 'under what identity and terms was the document obtained'. Together they cover the full chain from operator identity through capture conditions to text position, which is more provenance than any current injection defence requires and enough to support an auditable claim about how a stored artifact was acquired. Recording the signature key id and the response's access outcome per capture is cheap and belongs in the peripheral.
roundtrip_safety: RFC 9421's covered-component canonicalisation IS a serialisation fixed-point requirement, and a strict one: signer and verifier must derive byte-identical signature bases from the same request, or verification fails. That is a real-world example of a roundtrip-safety contract with an unforgiving oracle — any ambiguity in the encoding shows up immediately as a verification failure rather than as silent corruption. It is a useful model for the project's own escaping policy: define canonicalisation precisely, make divergence fail loudly, and never let two serialisations of the same content be considered equivalent.
token_budget_and_ordering: No effect on the SLM context. The Signature Agent Card is a small JSON document that should never enter the fold — it is metadata about the reader, not content from the page. The one budget-relevant point is that access outcome (signed/unsigned, verified/unverified, 200/402/challenged) should surface as an early marker in whatever the model receives, for the same reason gate state should: a model reasoning over a 402 stub or a licensing notice without knowing it is one will confidently describe the wrong document.
representation_cost: Three headers per request, on the order of a few hundred bytes; one small JSON card and one JWKS hosted once. Nothing enters the SLM context. In tokens the cost is exactly zero, which makes it the cheapest item in this research set by a wide margin relative to what it buys.
what_could_be_adopted: Adoptable, and it is the strongest positive recommendation in this research set — with the caveat that its short-term value on an archive-leaning corpus is small and its long-term value is structural. Four concrete pieces. (1) Sign requests: generate an Ed25519 key pair, host a JWKS at /.well-known/http-message-signature-directory, send Signature-Agent, Signature-Input (with the web-bot-auth tag) and Signature per RFC 9421. This is a small amount of code with no fidelity cost. (2) Publish a truthful minimal Signature Agent Card at /.well-known/signature-agent-card declaring client_name, contacts, trigger (this project's sensor is closer to 'fetcher' than 'crawler' when driven from a REPL, and that distinction should be declared honestly rather than chosen for advantage), purpose, and rfc9309-compliance stating which robots.txt directives are actually honoured — which requires actually honouring them. (3) Record the access outcome per capture as gate state, using the signature as the thing that makes 200 / 402 / challenged / degraded distinguishable. (4) Adopt the canonicalisation discipline as a model for the project's own serialisation contract. Crucially, adopting (1) and (2) is what makes the project's refusal of stealth tooling and its acceptance of Marionette coherent: it declares what it is instead of concealing or half-concealing it.
constraint_violation_ledger: structure_agnosticism: ADOPTABLE AS-IS — a transport mechanism that reads no page structure and names no region. no_layout_in_the_fold: ADOPTABLE AS-IS — no geometry at any point. o_delta: ADOPTABLE AS-IS — per-request constant cost, independent of page size, no incremental structure to maintain, no out-of-model change class on the client side. no_mocks: ADOPTABLE AS-IS and actively reinforcing — this is the anti-stealth technology, asserting a true identity rather than a false environment, so it is the one item in the privacy category that strengthens the no-mocks commitment instead of straining it. closed_shadow_roots_stay_closed: ADOPTABLE AS-IS, and it is the mechanism that repairs the constraint's justification — by declaring agency it removes detectability as a live concern for both the Marionette exposure and the attachShadow question, leaving the refusal standing on encapsulation, page-stability and maintenance grounds where it is sound. Overall verdict: ADOPTABLE AS-IS, and recommended, with two honest caveats — the standard is a single vendor's unadopted draft whose card schema will change, and the content-differentiation risk (origins serving verified agents reduced pages) is real, unmeasured, and should be measured before signing is made unconditional.
governance_signal_handling: This IS the governance layer's identity primitive, and it is what makes the rest of the stack enforceable. robots.txt, ai.txt, Content Signals and AIPREF all express preferences keyed to an agent identity that, before Web Bot Auth, was an unverifiable User-Agent string anyone could claim — which is why the entire preference layer has been advisory. The card's rfc9309-product-token and rfc9309-compliance fields bind a cryptographic identity to a robots.txt token and to a declaration of which directives are honoured, which is the first mechanism that could make a robots.txt rule mean something. HTTP 402 pay-per-crawl depends on it directly: charging requires knowing who to charge, and Cloudflare's pay-per-crawl is built on exactly this identity substrate. The strategic reading is that Web Bot Auth is the keystone of the whole governance category — items 12, 13 and 14 of this research set are downstream of it — and that a project intending to honour any of those signals should implement this one first, because without it the honouring is unverifiable and therefore worth nothing to the origin.
legal_basis_and_pii_posture: Materially improves the project's position and this is not a marginal effect. Under EDPB Guidelines 03/2026, where persistent storage of scraped content is the regulated act and legitimate interest turns on a balancing test, three things weigh heavily: transparency toward the publisher and data subjects, the reasonableness of their expectations, and whether the collection respected expressed preferences. A signed, identified, contactable agent publishing a card that states its purpose and its robots.txt compliance is close to the best available evidence on all three — it converts an anonymous crawl into a documented, attributable one with a named contact and a declared purpose, which is precisely what a legitimate-interest assessment asks for. It also creates real obligations: a published purpose that the project then exceeds is a documented misrepresentation, and the contacts field creates a channel through which objections must actually be handled. The card carries no PII beyond the operator's contact address, which is deliberate and appropriate. The net is a strongly favourable trade — accept accountability, gain a defensible lawful-basis story — and it is the same trade the project already makes elsewhere by preferring loud failure to quiet degradation.
